chunks: Al-Kafi: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The one who recites a hundred verses in his prayers at night - Allah Mighty and Majestic records for him devotion of the whole night (in reward) for it. The one who recites two hundred verses [at night] outside (his) prayers - the Qur’an will not dispute against him on the Day of Judgment. And the one who recites five hundred verses (total) in his prayers by day and at night - Allah Mighty and Majestic records for him in the Preserved Tablet a Qinṭār of good-deeds, and a Qinṭār is a thousand and two hundred Ūqiyya, and a (single) Ūqiyya is greater than the mountain of Uhud

key_terms.أُوقِيَّةٌ: An Ūqiyya, a unit of weight, smaller than a Qinṭār
key_terms.قُنُوتَ لَيْلَةٍ: Devotion or standing in prayer throughout the night
key_terms.قِنطَارًا: A Qinṭār, a large unit of weight or measure for good deeds
key_terms.لَمْ يُحَاجْهُ الْقُرْآنُ: The Quran will not dispute/argue against him (on Judgment Day)

ai.seo_question: What are the rewards for reciting 100, 200, and 500 verses of the Quran according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi emphasizes the cumulative spiritual merit of Quranic recitation, distinguishing between the intercessory 'Qunut' granted for night prayer recitation and the direct preservation of deeds in the Preserved Tablet (Al-Lawh Al-Mahfuz) for extensive daily recitation. Scholarly tradition interprets the 'Qantar' (a massive weight of gold) as a metaphorical for the overwhelming magnitude of divine reward, while the 'Qunut' signifies a state of supplication where the Quran itself advocates for the reciter on the Day of Judgment.
